title: Joining a Leisure Centre

lines.text: Good morning, Riverside Leisure Centre, Fiona speaking. How can I help?
Hi, I'm thinking of joining, and I wanted to ask a few questions about membership first, if that's okay.
Of course. Would you like me to take some details as we go? Then I can set up a free trial pass for you.
That would be great.
Lovely. Could I have your full name?
Yes, it's Marcus Eldridge. That's E-L-D-R-I-D-G-E.
Thank you. And what's the best number to contact you on?
My mobile, which is oh seven nine six two, four one eight, five five three.

Great. Now, we have three types of membership. There's the Standard, which covers the gym and the pool; the Off-Peak, which is the same facilities but only before four in the afternoon on weekdays; and the Premium, which adds all the fitness classes and the sauna.
I see. I work shifts, so I was going to say Off-Peak, but actually some weeks I'm only free in the evenings. How much is the Standard?
The Standard is thirty-four pounds a month. Off-Peak is twenty-two, and Premium is forty-nine.
Hmm. I do like the idea of the classes, but realistically I'd mainly use the pool. I'll go with the Standard.
Sensible. There's normally a joining fee of twenty pounds, but this month we're waiving it for anyone who signs up for twelve months.
Oh, that's handy. Is there a minimum contract otherwise?
If you don't take the twelve-month option, it's a rolling monthly contract, but you need to give us one month's notice to cancel.
Okay, I'll think about the twelve months. What about parking? I've heard it can be a nightmare.
It used to be, but we've opened a new car park behind the tennis courts, so that's eased things a lot. Members get two hours free; you just enter your registration at the desk.
Brilliant. And one more thing. Do I need to book an induction before I can use the gym?
Yes, everyone has a short induction with one of our instructors. It takes about forty minutes. The next available slots are Tuesday at six or Thursday at half past seven.
Tuesday's no good, I'm working late. Thursday, please.
Thursday at seven thirty, then. Please bring a towel and a water bottle, and wear trainers. No outdoor shoes on the gym floor.
Got it. Should I bring any identification?
Yes, some photo ID. And if you've got any medical conditions we should know about, there's a short health questionnaire, which you can fill in online beforehand to save time.
Perfect. Thanks so much for your help.
You're welcome, Marcus. See you on Thursday.

title: A Tour of Harwood Mill

lines.text: Right, good morning everyone, and welcome to Harwood Mill. My name's Tom and I'll be your guide for the next hour or so. Before we start, just a few practical things. The toilets are straight ahead, past the ticket desk, and the café is on your left as you came in, opposite the gift shop.

Now, the mill was built in eighteen twenty-four to spin cotton, and at its peak it employed around six hundred people, many of them children, which is something we'll come back to later. It closed in nineteen sixty-eight, and for nearly thirty years the building was more or less abandoned.

We'll begin here on the ground floor, in the engine house. This enormous steam engine is the original one, and it still works. We fire it up on the first Sunday of every month, so if you're interested, it's well worth coming back for that.

From here, we'll take the stairs up to the weaving hall on the first floor. There's a lift as well, by the way, at the far end of the corridor, if anyone would prefer that. In the weaving hall you'll see the looms, and one of our volunteers will show you how they work. Fair warning: they're incredibly loud, so we provide ear defenders.

I should mention that the dye house, which is normally in the basement, is closed this month while the floor is being repaired. Instead, we've put a small display about dyeing in the corridor next to the lift, so you won't miss out entirely.
Sorry, can I ask, is there anything for younger children? My two are six and eight.

Absolutely. The family activity room used to be in the courtyard, but it's moved into the old manager's office, which is the small brick building beside the car park. There are costumes, puzzles and a mini loom they can actually use.
Oh, they'll love that. Thanks.

No problem. Then, after the weaving hall, we'll go up to the top floor, where there's an exhibition called Small Hands, about the lives of child workers. It's quite moving, I think, and it's based on letters and diaries we found when the building was restored.

And we'll finish on the riverside terrace, where you can see the water wheel that powered the mill before the steam engine was installed. On a clear day you get a lovely view of the valley from there. Any questions so far? No? Right, follow me.

title: Tutorial: A Group Project

lines.text: Come in, Liam. So, you wanted to talk about the group project on community gardens?
Yes, thanks for seeing me. We've made a start, but we're a bit stuck on the methodology.
Okay. Remind me what your research question is.
Basically, whether people who take part in community gardens feel more connected to their neighbourhood than people who don't.
Good, that's nicely focused. And how were you planning to collect data?
Originally we wanted to do face-to-face interviews with about fifty gardeners, but when we worked it out, that would take far too long. So now we're thinking of an online questionnaire instead.
That's reasonable, although I'd keep a few interviews too. Questionnaires give you numbers, but interviews tell you why people feel the way they do. Even five or six would add a lot of depth.
That makes sense. Maybe Hannah could do those. She's the most confident at that sort of thing.
And who are you comparing the gardeners with?
People living in the same streets who don't garden. We were going to knock on doors, but...
I'd be careful there. You'll need ethics approval for door-to-door contact, and that can take weeks. It might be easier to recruit through the local library or a community noticeboard.
Oh, I hadn't thought about ethics. Is the form complicated?
Not really, it's about four pages. Submit it by the end of next week, though, because the committee only meets once a month.
Right. The other problem is that one of our group members, Sam, hasn't really been contributing.

That happens more than you'd think. My advice is to give everyone a clear role and write it down. If there's still no change, come and see me, and we'll look at the peer assessment, which is worth twenty per cent of the mark.
Okay. And for the final report, is the word limit strict?
It's three thousand words, and we allow ten per cent either way. The reference list doesn't count, but the tables do, so keep them simple.
Got it. Oh, and should we include photos of the gardens?
You can, but put them in an appendix rather than the main text. And remember to get permission if there are people in them.
Brilliant. That's really helpful. I think we know what to do now.
Good. Send me a draft of the questionnaire before you put it online, and I'll have a quick look.

title: Two Flats, One Decision

lines.text: Okay, so we've seen both flats now. Which one are you leaning towards?
Honestly? I walked out of the Marlow Road one thinking it was perfect, but the more I think about it, the less sure I am.
Really? I thought you loved it. The living room was huge.

It was. And the rent is lower, thirteen hundred and fifty a month compared to fifteen hundred for the one near the station. But it's a forty-minute bus ride to my office, and the buses only run every twenty minutes.
Hmm, true. For me it doesn't make much difference, because I work from home three days a week.
Exactly, so it's me who'd be stuck on the bus. Whereas from the station flat I could walk to work in fifteen minutes.
But the second bedroom there is tiny. Whoever gets it would barely fit a bed and a desk.
I'd take the small room if we went for that one. I don't need much space.
That's generous of you. Though if we're splitting the rent equally, that's not really fair on you.
Well, we could split it differently. Maybe I pay a bit less?
Yeah, that seems reasonable. What about the washing machine? Marlow Road didn't have one.
The agent said the landlord might put one in, but might isn't very reassuring. And the station flat has one, plus a dishwasher.

You'd be having breakfast next to a railway line, mind you.

Me neither. They said the windows were replaced last year, so that helps.

Supposedly. But the station flat is in a newer building, so it's probably better insulated. I'd guess the bills come out about the same.

And the garden, to be fair. But neither of us has time to look after a garden.

title: What Keeps Us Awake?

lines.text: Welcome back to Everyday Science, the podcast where we take the things you do every day and ask what's actually going on. I'm Nadia, and today we're talking about sleep with Dr Ben Carter, who runs a sleep lab at a university hospital. Ben, thanks for coming in.
Thanks for having me. It's a topic people always have strong opinions about.
They really do. Let's start with the big one: screens. Everyone says the blue light from our phones keeps us awake. Is that true?

Partly. Blue light does affect the hormone that makes us sleepy, but the effect from a phone is actually fairly small. What matters more, in our research, is what you're doing on the screen. If you're answering work emails or arguing with someone online, your brain stays alert. Reading a calm article is much less of a problem.
So it's the content, not the light.
Mostly, yes. Although I'd still say put the phone down half an hour before bed if you can.
What about naps? I love a nap, but I've heard they can ruin your night.

They can, if you get them wrong. A short nap, around twenty minutes, can really boost concentration. The problems start when people sleep for an hour or more, or nap late in the afternoon. As a rule of thumb, I'd say finish any nap before three o'clock.
Good to know. Now, a lot of our listeners are students, and they often say they simply can't fall asleep before midnight.
And they're not being lazy! During adolescence the body clock genuinely shifts later, by up to two hours. That's why some researchers argue that schools should start later in the morning.
Interesting. And what about catching up at the weekend? I sleep until eleven on Saturdays.

That's very common, but it creates what we call social jet lag. Your body thinks it's travelled to a different time zone, and then on Monday morning you have to fly back, so to speak. Keeping your wake-up time within about an hour of your weekday time is much better.
Ouch. Okay, last question: coffee. I usually have one at about four o'clock.
Caffeine stays in your system longer than people realise. Roughly half of it is still there five or six hours later. So that four o'clock coffee is still partly active at ten at night.
I think I need to rethink my afternoons. Ben, thank you so much.
My pleasure. Sleep well, everyone.

title: E-Bikes: Six Months On

lines.text: Now, it's been six months since the city launched its electric bike-sharing scheme, and opinions are still divided. Our transport correspondent, James Whitby, has been finding out how it's going.

Thanks, Claire. I'm standing at one of the busiest docking stations, outside the central library, and in the ten minutes I've been here, at least a dozen bikes have been taken out. According to the council, there have been around a hundred and eighty thousand journeys since the launch in April, well above the original target of a hundred and twenty thousand.

The bikes cost a pound to unlock, plus fifteen pence per minute, although there's a monthly pass for twelve pounds, which gives you unlimited rides of up to forty-five minutes. Ruth Adeyemi, a nurse, uses the scheme every day.

I used to drive to the hospital, but parking was costing me a fortune, and honestly I was always stressed. Now I cycle, and it takes about the same time. The electric motor makes the hill on Station Road manageable, which it never was on my old bike.

Not everyone is so enthusiastic, though. Some residents have complained that bikes are being left on pavements, blocking the way for wheelchair users and people with pushchairs. Ruth admits she's seen it too.
Yes, it's a real problem in some areas. I think people should be fined if they don't return the bike to a proper station. At the moment, I don't think there's any penalty at all.

In fact, the council says that from next month, users who leave bikes outside the official parking zones will be charged an extra five pounds. They're also planning to add thirty new docking stations, mainly in the suburbs, which at the moment are poorly served.

There have also been concerns about safety. Two of the city's main roads still don't have separate cycle lanes, and a local campaign group says that's putting people off. The council has promised to build them, but hasn't yet said when.
That's the main thing that would get more people cycling, in my view. I'm fairly confident on the roads, but my sister won't even try it.
So, a promising start, but clearly some problems to fix. Back to you, Claire.
Thanks, James.

title: Festival Volunteer Briefing

lines.text: Hi everyone, and thanks so much for volunteering at this year's Greenfield Folk Festival. I know some of you have done this before and some of you are completely new, so I'll go through the essentials, and then you'll meet your team leaders.

First, shifts. Each of you will do three shifts of six hours over the weekend, and in return you get a free weekend ticket and meals on the days you're working. Your rota should be in your welcome pack, but if it's missing, go to the volunteer tent, which is the green one next to the main car park, not the white one by the stage. That's first aid.

Please arrive at least fifteen minutes before your shift starts so you can sign in. We used to ask for half an hour, but people told us it was too much, so we've cut it down. If you're going to be late, or you're ill, text your team leader rather than calling, because it's often too noisy to hear the phone.

Now, roles. Most of you will be in one of three areas: the entrance gates, checking tickets and wristbands; the recycling team, which is honestly the hardest work, but people say it's the most fun; or the information point, answering questions from the public. If you've got a preference, tell your team leader today and we'll try to accommodate it, but I can't promise anything.

A few rules. You must wear your volunteer T-shirt during every shift, so people can find you. Alcohol is obviously not allowed while you're working, and that includes breaks. And please don't post photos of the backstage area on social media. The artists really value their privacy.

Safety is the big one. If you see someone who looks unwell, don't try to deal with it yourself; radio the control room, or send someone to the first aid tent. And if there's ever an announcement asking people to leave a particular area, your job is to stay calm and point people towards the nearest exit, which will be marked with yellow flags.
Last thing: the weather forecast for Saturday isn't great, so bring waterproofs and sensible boots. Trust me, the fields turn into mud very quickly.
Right, any questions before we split into teams? No? Okay, team leaders, they're all yours.

title: Interview: Events Coordinator

lines.text: Diego, thanks for coming in. Please, have a seat.
Thank you. It's nice to meet you.
So, as you know, this is for the events coordinator role. Could you start by telling me a bit about your current job?

Sure. I've been working at a conference centre for about three years, mainly in customer service, but for the last eighteen months I've been helping to organise smaller events: company training days, a couple of weddings, that kind of thing.
And what made you apply for this position?

Well, I really enjoy the planning side, and at the moment it's only part of my job. Here it would be the main focus. Also, to be honest, the hotel's reputation for weddings was a big attraction. I'd like to specialise in that area eventually.
Good. Can you tell me about a time when something went wrong at an event, and how you dealt with it?

Yes. Last spring we had a training day for about eighty people, and that morning the caterers phoned to say their van had broken down. Lunch was going to be at least two hours late. At first I panicked a little, I'll admit, but then I called a local bakery we'd worked with before, and they delivered sandwiches within forty minutes. I also moved the afternoon coffee break earlier so nobody went hungry.
That's resourceful. How did the client react?
They were actually very happy. They booked with us again in the autumn.
Excellent. Now, this role involves a lot of weekend work, especially from May to September. Would that be a problem?

title: Should Homework Go?

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Open Question. Tonight's motion is: homework should be abolished in primary schools. Speaking for the motion is Paul Hughes, a head teacher, and against it is Rosa Mendez, an education researcher. Paul, you first.

Thank you. I've been teaching for over twenty years, and I used to set homework every night without thinking about it. But when we looked at the research properly, we found very little evidence that homework improves results for children under eleven. What it does do is create stress and arguments at home, and it disadvantages children whose parents work long hours or don't speak English. So three years ago, my school stopped setting it, apart from reading.
And what happened?
Our test results stayed exactly the same, but parents reported far fewer arguments, and children had more time for sport, music and simply playing outside, which matters enormously at that age.
Rosa, how do you respond?

Well, first, I agree with Paul that a lot of homework is poorly designed. Worksheets that just keep children busy are pointless. But I don't accept that the answer is to get rid of it altogether. Short, well-planned tasks help children develop independence and the habit of studying, which they'll badly need at secondary school.
But they can develop those habits at school, during the day.
To some extent. But there's another benefit: homework is often the only window parents have into what their child is learning. If you remove it, many families lose that connection.
Paul, that's a fair point, isn't it?

It is, and we did worry about that. So now we send home a weekly newsletter explaining what each class is studying, with suggestions for things families can do together, like cooking or visiting a museum, if they want to. The key word is if.
That sounds lovely, but I'd argue it actually increases inequality rather than reducing it. The families with time and money will do those activities; others won't.
Whereas with compulsory homework, the children without support at home simply fail to do it and get into trouble. I'd say that's worse.
So, is there any common ground?
I think we both agree that reading at home is valuable, and that quantity isn't the point. Ten minutes of meaningful practice beats an hour of busywork.
Yes, I'd go along with that.
Let's take some questions from the audience.

title: Why We Waste Food at Home

lines.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at household food waste, which is something most of us contribute to without really noticing. When people think about food waste, they tend to imagine supermarkets or restaurants throwing away huge quantities of food. And those are certainly part of the picture. But in many wealthy countries, the largest share of waste, often more than half, actually comes from households.

So why do we waste so much at home? Researchers usually point to three main causes. The first is over-buying. Special offers, like buy one, get one free, encourage us to purchase more than we can realistically eat. The second is poor storage. A surprising number of people keep fruit and vegetables in the wrong place, so they go off much faster than they should. And the third, which is the one I find most interesting, is confusion about date labels.

Let me explain. In many countries, food packaging has two different kinds of date. A use by date is about safety: after that date, the food might make you ill, so you shouldn't eat it. A best before date, on the other hand, is only about quality. After that date, the food might be a little less fresh or crunchy, but it's perfectly safe. Surveys suggest that around a third of consumers don't understand the difference, and they throw away food that is completely fine.

Now, some countries have started to tackle this. A few supermarkets have removed best before dates from fresh fruit and vegetables entirely, encouraging customers to use their own judgement, to look at the food and smell it. Early results seem positive, although it's too soon to say whether the effect will last.

Another approach is technology. There are apps that let neighbours share surplus food, and some fridges now have cameras inside, so you can check what you've got while you're at the shop. Personally, I'm a bit sceptical about the fridges. They're expensive, and I suspect most people won't use the feature after the first few weeks. The sharing apps seem more promising, particularly in cities.

Finally, it's worth remembering why this matters. When food is wasted, so is all the water, energy and land used to produce it. And when it ends up in landfill, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
For next week, I'd like you to keep a simple food diary, recording everything you throw away for seven days, and why. We'll compare results in the seminar.

title: Cities That Trap Heat

lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is on what's known as the urban heat island effect: the phenomenon whereby cities are noticeably warmer than the countryside around them. On a still summer night, the difference can be as much as seven or eight degrees, which, as you can imagine, has serious implications for health, for energy use and, increasingly, for how we design cities.

So what causes it? There isn't a single explanation; rather, several factors reinforce one another. The most obvious is the materials we build with. Asphalt, concrete and brick absorb solar radiation during the day and then release it slowly at night, which is why the effect tends to be strongest after dark, not, as people often assume, at midday.

Second, cities have far less vegetation. Trees and plants cool their surroundings through a process called evapotranspiration. Essentially, they release water vapour, and that uses up heat energy. Remove them, and you lose a natural air-conditioning system. Third, there's the geometry of the city itself. Tall buildings on narrow streets create what are sometimes called urban canyons, which trap heat and reduce wind. And finally there's waste heat from human activity: vehicles, industry and, ironically, air conditioners, which pump hot air outside in order to cool the inside.

Now, why should we care? The most pressing issue is health. During heatwaves, mortality rates in cities rise sharply, and the people most at risk are the elderly, those with existing heart or lung conditions, and people living alone. It's worth stressing that the danger isn't only daytime temperatures; it's the lack of relief at night. If the body can't cool down while you sleep, the strain accumulates over several days.

So what can be done? Broadly speaking, the solutions fall into three groups. The first is greening: planting street trees, creating parks and installing green roofs. Trees are probably the single most cost-effective measure, though they take years to mature, so it's a long-term investment.

The second is what we might call cool materials. Painting roofs white or using reflective paving can lower surface temperatures considerably. Some cities have trialled this with encouraging results, although I should add a note of caution: reflective surfaces at street level can increase glare and actually make pedestrians feel hotter, because the sunlight bounces back up at them. So it's not a straightforward win.

The third group concerns design and planning: orienting streets to channel breezes, for instance, or restoring rivers that were buried under roads in the last century. That's far more expensive and disruptive, of course, but the cities that have done it, often for other reasons such as flood management, have seen measurable cooling benefits.

To my mind, the key point is that none of these measures is sufficient on its own. The cities making real progress are those combining approaches and, crucially, targeting the neighbourhoods that need them most, which are very often the poorer ones with the fewest trees.
In the seminar on Thursday we'll look at a case study from a southern European city that mapped surface temperatures street by street, so please read the article on the reading list beforehand.

title: Dissertation Tutorial: Code-Switching

lines.text: Come in, Lucía. Have a seat. So, I've read through your proposal. Shall we start with your overall impressions of how it's going, and then I'll give you my thoughts?
Sure. Honestly, I feel quite positive about the topic, but I'm less confident about the methodology. I keep changing my mind.
That's perfectly normal at this stage. Remind me of the core question.

I'm looking at code-switching among bilingual teenagers, so when and why they move between Spanish and English in the same conversation. Specifically, whether it's mostly about filling gaps in vocabulary, or whether it's doing something social, like signalling identity.

Right. It's a genuinely interesting question, because the older literature tended to treat code-switching as a sign of deficiency, whereas more recent work sees it as a skill. So you're entering a live debate, which is good.
That's what drew me to it. My plan was to use a questionnaire asking students when they switch languages and why.

Mm. I'd question that a little. The difficulty with self-report is that people are often unaware of when they code-switch. They may tell you they only do it when they forget a word, but recordings frequently show otherwise. So there's a risk your data would reflect people's beliefs about their behaviour rather than the behaviour itself.
So I should record conversations instead?

Not necessarily instead. I think the strongest design would combine the two: record some natural conversations, then compare what you observe with what the same speakers say they do. The gap between the two could actually become one of your findings.
Oh, I like that. Although recording is going to be much harder to organise, and I'd need consent from parents, since they're under eighteen.
You would, and that's not trivial. How many participants were you thinking of?
For the questionnaire, I was hoping for around a hundred, but for recordings that seems unrealistic.

It is. Transcribing just one hour of conversation can take six or seven hours. I'd suggest something like eight to ten pairs of friends, recorded for about twenty minutes each. That's manageable, and it's a qualitative study, so depth matters more than numbers.
Okay. And what did you think of the literature review?

It's thorough, but at the moment it reads rather like a list: this author said this, that author said that. What I'd like to see is more synthesis: grouping the studies by theme, showing where they disagree, and then positioning your own study in that gap.
That's fair. I did feel it was a bit descriptive.
One more thing: be careful about the term Spanglish. Some speakers use it proudly; others find it dismissive. If you use it, define it and acknowledge that it's contested.
Good point. I hadn't thought about that.

And in terms of timing, I'd aim to submit your ethics application within the next fortnight, because the recordings can't start without approval, and schools tend to be less flexible in the summer term.
Right. So, ethics first, then contact schools, then rework the literature review while I'm waiting.
Exactly. You've got a solid project here, Lucía. It just needs a bit of tightening.

title: Remembering What Never Happened

lines.text: Hello and welcome to Mind Matters. I'm Joel Barker, and today we're talking about memory, and specifically why our memories are far less reliable than we'd like to believe. My guest is cognitive psychologist Dr Imogen Clarke. Imogen, welcome.
Thanks, Joel. Lovely to be here.
So, let's start with the basic idea. I think most people imagine memory as a kind of video recording. Is that wrong?

It's an understandable assumption, but yes, it's pretty much wrong. Memory is reconstructive. Every time you recall an event, you're essentially rebuilding it from fragments, and in the process you can fill in gaps with things you expect, or things you've heard since. So the act of remembering can itself change the memory.
That's slightly unsettling.
It is, a bit. But it's also quite efficient. Storing every detail would be enormously costly for the brain. It makes sense to keep the gist and reconstruct the rest.
Now, you've done research on what are called false memories. Can you explain what that means?

Sure. A false memory isn't simply getting a detail wrong, like the colour of someone's coat. It's remembering, often vividly, something that never happened at all. In some well-known experiments, researchers showed participants doctored photographs, say, of themselves as a child in a hot-air balloon, and after a few interviews, a substantial minority started recalling the balloon ride, sometimes with sensory details.
Wow. And these are ordinary, healthy people?
Completely. And I think that's the crucial point. People tend to assume false memories are a sign of something being wrong, but they're a by-product of a system that's working normally.
Does confidence tell us anything? If I'm absolutely certain I remember something...

Less than you'd hope. Confidence and accuracy are only loosely related, particularly for memories that have been retold many times. The more often you tell a story, the more fluent and confident it becomes, but not necessarily more accurate. In some cases, it drifts further from what actually happened.
Which has huge implications for, say, eyewitness testimony in court.

Enormous. Historically, juries have found confident eyewitnesses extremely persuasive, and there have been cases of people being wrongly convicted largely on that basis. Things have improved. Police in many places now record an eyewitness's confidence at the very first identification, before it can be inflated by feedback. That initial confidence turns out to be a much better guide.
Interesting. So it's not that confidence is useless; it's about when you measure it.
Exactly. That's a nice way of putting it.
Before we finish, is there anything listeners can do to protect their memories?

Well, I'd be wary of anyone promising a technique to make memory perfectly accurate. That's not how it works. But if something important happens, writing it down soon afterwards, before you've discussed it with others, helps a lot. And maybe a little humility. When you disagree with a friend about what happened at a party five years ago, it's quite possible you're both wrong.
I'll remember that. Or at least, I'll think I do. Imogen Clarke, thank you.

title: Rewilding: Who Decides?

lines.text: Welcome to The Debate Room. Tonight we're discussing rewilding: the idea of allowing large areas of land to return to a more natural state, sometimes including the reintroduction of species like beavers or even lynx. With me are ecologist Dr Mia Torres and sheep farmer Gareth Lloyd. Mia, let's start with you. What's the case for rewilding?

Thanks, Elena. The case, quite simply, is that we're losing biodiversity at an alarming rate, and conventional conservation, protecting small, isolated reserves, hasn't been enough to reverse that. Rewilding takes a different approach. Rather than managing every detail, we restore natural processes and let them do the work. Beavers are a good example: their dams slow rivers down, create wetlands, and in several trial areas they've reduced flooding downstream.
Gareth, you're sceptical.

I am, though perhaps not for the reasons people expect. I'm not against nature. I wouldn't be farming if I were. My concern is that rewilding is often driven by people who don't live in the places affected. Land gets bought up by wealthy investors, sometimes to offset their carbon emissions, and the farms that kept rural communities alive disappear. The school closes, the shop closes. That's a real cost, and it's rarely discussed.

I think that's a completely legitimate concern, and I'd agree that some projects have handled it badly. But rewilding doesn't have to mean removing people. Some of the most successful schemes involve farmers directly. They're paid to manage land for wildlife alongside producing food.
In theory. In practice, the payments are often short-term, and you can't plan a farm business around a scheme that might be cancelled in three years.
What about predators? The reintroduction of lynx has been very controversial.

That's where I'd draw the line, frankly. My neighbours and I have enough trouble with foxes and stray dogs. Supporters say lynx rarely take sheep, and maybe that's true elsewhere, but our sheep graze on open hillsides, not in fields, so I'm not convinced the evidence transfers.

That's fair, and I'd actually say lynx are the wrong place to start in most areas. Public trust matters. If you begin with something divisive, you can set the whole movement back. Starting with beavers or restoring wetlands builds confidence. Then, if communities want to, you can look at bigger steps, with proper compensation for any losses.
Gareth, is there any form of rewilding you could support?

Yes, actually. Planting hedgerows, leaving field margins wild, letting some wetter ground go back to bog. A lot of farmers are doing that already, without calling it rewilding. What I object to is the idea that farming and nature are opposites. On our farm, we've seen more birds in the last five years, not fewer.

And I think that's where the conversation should go. The label rewilding has become a bit of a battleground, which is unhelpful. If we talked more about outcomes, like cleaner rivers, more insects and fewer floods, I suspect we'd find we agree on more than we disagree on.
I'd go along with that. As long as the people who live on the land have a genuine say.
On that note of cautious agreement, let's take some questions from our audience.

title: Riders, Rights and the Apps

lines.text: The number of people working for app-based delivery platforms has more than doubled in the past five years, and a court ruling this week could change the way they're employed. Ayesha Khan has been looking into it.

Thanks, Hugh. It's just after seven on a Friday evening, and outside this row of restaurants there must be fifteen or twenty couriers waiting for orders, most of them on electric bikes or mopeds. One of them, Marek, has been doing this for nearly four years.

When I started, it was good money, honestly. You could earn more than in a warehouse, and you choose your hours. That freedom is still the best part. But the pay per delivery has gone down, maybe by a quarter, and there are many more riders now, so you wait longer between jobs. Some evenings I earn less than the minimum wage, once you take away fuel and insurance.

At the heart of the issue is employment status. Couriers like Marek are classified as self-employed contractors, which means they aren't entitled to holiday pay, sick pay or a pension. The platforms argue that this is what gives workers flexibility. In a statement, one of the largest companies told us that the overwhelming majority of its riders value being able to log on and off whenever they choose, and that guaranteed hours would inevitably mean less choice.

Flexibility, yes, I want this. But flexibility and some protection are not opposites. If I'm injured on the road, and I've had two accidents, I earn nothing while I recover. That's not freedom, that's risk.

This week's ruling concerned a group of couriers who argued that, because the app controls which orders they receive and can deactivate their accounts without explanation, they are in practice workers rather than independent contractors. The court agreed, at least partially. It didn't go as far as declaring them employees, but it said they should be entitled to holiday pay and a minimum hourly rate for the time they're logged in and available.

Employment lawyers I've spoken to are cautious about how far-reaching this will be. The ruling applies directly to only one company, and that company has already said it intends to appeal. One lawyer told me the platforms are likely to respond by changing their contracts, for instance by allowing riders to send a substitute to do a delivery, which could weaken the argument that riders are personally controlled by the app.
And what about customers? Could this push up prices?

Almost certainly a little, though economists disagree on how much. Some argue that higher costs will reduce demand and therefore the number of jobs. Others point out that similar rules elsewhere haven't caused the collapse that was predicted. Marek, for his part, is unconvinced by the warnings.
They always say if we get rights, the business will die. They said the same about the minimum wage. I don't think people will stop ordering pizza because it costs fifty pence more.
The appeal is expected to be heard early next year. Until then, for Marek and thousands like him, very little will change. Hugh.
Ayesha Khan, thank you.

title: Inside the Botanic Garden

lines.text: Okay, if everyone could gather round. That's it, come a bit closer so you can hear me over the fountain. Welcome to the Halden Botanic Garden. I'm Kirra, and I'll be taking you round for about an hour and a quarter. We'll finish at the seed vault, which, for many people, is the highlight, although I'll admit I'm slightly biased, because I used to work there.

We're standing on what we call the Compass Lawn, and if you look at the map in your leaflet, you'll see the garden is laid out roughly by continent. To the north, beyond the glasshouses, is the Asian collection; the Americas are to the east, over the bridge; and directly behind me, to the south, is the Australasian section, which, as an Australian, I'm obliged to tell you is the best one.

We'll start with the Palm House, the large Victorian glasshouse on your left. It was completed in eighteen fifty-nine, and at the time it was one of the most ambitious iron-and-glass structures in the world. It's kept at around twenty-seven degrees and it's very humid, so you might want to take off a layer before we go in. Glasses tend to steam up, too. Sorry in advance.

Inside, keep an eye out for the giant water lily in the central pond. Its leaves can grow to over two metres across, and the underside has a network of ribs that's so strong, it reportedly inspired the design of the building itself. Whether that story's entirely true is debatable, to be honest, but it's a good one.

After the Palm House, we'll walk along the Long Border. In spring it's spectacular, but at this time of year it's mostly being cut back, so we won't linger. Then we'll cross the bridge to the Americas section. Please stay on the paths there. We're re-establishing a meadow, and it's more delicate than it looks.
Sorry, is the treetop walkway open? I read that it was closed.

Good question. It was closed for most of the summer for repairs, but it reopened last week. It's not on the main tour because of time, but it's just beside the Americas section, and you're very welcome to go up afterwards. Last entry is half an hour before closing.
Great, thanks.

Then finally, we'll come to the seed vault. Now, this is where the garden's work goes far beyond being a pretty place to walk. The vault holds seeds from around forty thousand plant species, many of them endangered in the wild. The seeds are dried and stored at minus twenty degrees, and in those conditions many can survive for centuries. The idea is essentially an insurance policy: if a species disappears in the wild, we have the material to reintroduce it.

That said, I don't want to give the impression it's a perfect solution. Some seeds, including those of many tropical trees, oddly enough, can't survive being dried, so they can't be banked in this way. For those, we rely on living collections, or on newer techniques like freezing tiny pieces of plant tissue, which is still quite experimental.

You can't go inside the vault itself, I'm afraid, but there's a viewing window, and one of the scientists usually gives a short talk at three o'clock. Right, the Palm House. Follow me, and mind the step.

title: Building on What's There

lines.text: My guest today is the architect Kwame Asante, whose practice has become known for converting old industrial buildings rather than demolishing them. Kwame, thanks for joining me.
It's a pleasure.
Let's start with the obvious question. Why reuse? Surely it's often simpler to knock a building down and start again.

Simpler, perhaps, in the short term. But there's a growing recognition that the greenest building is usually the one that already exists. When you demolish, you throw away all the energy and carbon that went into making the steel, the concrete and the bricks, what we call embodied carbon. A new building, however efficient it is to run, can take decades to make up for that.
Is that always the case, though? Some old buildings are terribly inefficient.

That's true, and I'd never claim reuse is always right. If a structure is genuinely unsafe, or so poorly insulated that it can't be improved, then replacement might be justified. But in my experience, that's the exception. What's more common is that a developer simply hasn't investigated the options, because demolition is the default.
Your best-known project is the old tram depot that's now a library and housing. What were the main challenges there?

Oh, where to begin. The building had been empty for fifteen years, and the roof was leaking badly. But the biggest challenge was light. Tram depots are deep buildings with very few windows, which is fine for trams but not for people. We ended up cutting a long courtyard through the middle, which meant losing some floor space. The client was nervous about that at first, understandably, because floor space is money.
How did you persuade them?
Partly with numbers. We showed that brighter flats would rent for more. But honestly, what convinced them was a visit to a similar project in Rotterdam. Once they stood in the space, they understood.
Did local residents have any say?

Quite a lot, actually. We held workshops with people living nearby, and one thing that came out very strongly was that they wanted to keep the old tram tracks visible. Initially we'd planned to cover them, purely for practical reasons. But people had an emotional attachment; their grandparents had worked there. So we set them into the floor of the library under glass. It's become the thing everyone photographs.
That's lovely. Do you think the planning system makes this kind of work harder than it should be?

In some respects, yes. Building regulations are largely written with new buildings in mind, so you spend a lot of time proving that an old structure meets standards it was never designed for. I'm not arguing for lower safety standards, absolutely not, but there needs to be more flexibility in how you demonstrate them. And there's a tax issue: in many places, renovation is taxed more heavily than new construction, which is frankly absurd if we're serious about climate targets.
Finally, what advice would you give to young architects?

Learn to love constraints. Designing on an empty site is a fantasy most of us will rarely get. Working with what's there forces you to be more inventive, and I think the results are often richer for it.

title: Seminar: Honest Placebos

lines.text: Okay, let's get started. This week's reading was the paper on open-label placebos. Ollie, could you summarise it briefly for us?

Sure. So, normally, a placebo works because the patient thinks they're getting real medicine. This study tested what happens if you give people a placebo and tell them openly that it's a placebo, just a sugar pill with no active ingredient. The participants all had chronic back pain, and after three weeks, the group taking the open placebo reported significantly less pain than the group who just continued their usual treatment.
Thank you. Jade, what was your reaction?

Honestly, my first reaction was disbelief. It seems almost paradoxical: how can something work if you know it's fake? But having read it a couple of times, I'm more persuaded than I was. The researchers didn't just hand out pills; they explained to participants that placebos can trigger the body's own pain-relief mechanisms, and I think that explanation might be doing a lot of the work.
That's the bit I'm not sure about, though. If the explanation's the active ingredient, is it really a placebo effect, or is it more like a form of education or reassurance?
That's a sharp distinction. Does it matter, from a practical point of view?
Maybe not for the patient. But it matters scientifically, because it changes what we think is going on.

I'd also question the outcome measure. Everything was self-reported. Patients rated their own pain on a scale. Pain is subjective, so that's partly unavoidable, but there was no objective measure, like how far people could walk.
Good. So what would you want to see in a follow-up study?
Ideally, a comparison group who get the same friendly, detailed conversation but no pill. That would tell us whether the pill itself adds anything.

And a longer timescale. Three weeks is quite short. Chronic pain fluctuates naturally, so some improvement might have happened anyway. Although, to be fair, the control group would have experienced the same fluctuations, so that doesn't completely undermine the results.
Right, that's what the control group is for. What about the ethical side? Traditionally, the problem with placebos in clinical practice is that they involve deceiving patients.
Which is exactly why this is exciting, I think. If you can get a benefit without deception, then a lot of the ethical objections fall away. Doctors could potentially offer it honestly.

I'm a bit more cautious. I can imagine it being misused, for example by health systems offering placebos instead of properly investigating someone's pain, because it's cheap. Chronic pain patients already often feel they're not taken seriously.
That's an important point, and it's one the authors don't really address. Overall, then, where do you both stand?
Cautiously optimistic. It's a small study, just under a hundred participants, but the effect was large enough to be worth replicating properly.
I'd say intrigued but unconvinced. I'd want to see it replicated with objective measures before I took it too seriously.
That's a very healthy range of views. For next week, I'd like each of you to design, in outline, the follow-up study you've described today, and we'll compare them.

title: A Translator's Confession

lines.text: Thank you all for coming. When I was asked to talk about my work as a literary translator, my first instinct was to say no, because translators are supposed to be invisible. The highest compliment you can pay a translation, people often say, is that it doesn't read like one. I used to believe that completely. I'm less sure now, and that's partly what I want to talk about.

I started translating almost by accident. I was working in publishing, reading Spanish novels and writing reports on whether they might sell in English. One day an editor asked me to try a sample chapter, and that was it. That was twenty-two years ago now.

People tend to imagine translation as a matter of finding equivalent words. In fact, individual words are rarely the hard part. The difficulty lies in everything around them: rhythm, humour, the social weight of a particular expression. Take the difference between the formal and informal you in Spanish. English simply doesn't have it, so a moment where two characters shift from usted to tú, which in the original might be quietly romantic, or a sign of disrespect, can disappear entirely unless I find another way to signal it. Sometimes that means changing the way they address each other, or adding a small gesture. Every solution is a compromise.

Humour is even worse. A pun almost never survives. I once spent three days on a single joke in a children's book, and in the end I replaced it with a completely different joke that worked in English. Some readers would call that a betrayal. I'd call it faithfulness to the effect rather than the words: the original made children laugh, so the translation should too.

Now, about invisibility. For a long time, translators' names didn't appear on book covers at all, and in many cases they still don't. There's been a campaign recently to change that, and I support it, though not, I hope, out of vanity. It's more that hiding the translator encourages readers to believe they're reading the author's exact words, and that's never quite true. Every translation is an interpretation. I'd rather readers knew that.

Then, of course, there's the question everyone asks me these days: will machines replace us? I'd be lying if I said I wasn't worried at all. Machine translation has improved remarkably, and for instruction manuals or business emails it's often perfectly adequate. But literature is a different matter. A machine can produce a sentence that's grammatically flawless and still completely wrong in tone. What concerns me more, honestly, is economic pressure: publishers asking translators to just correct machine output for a fraction of the fee. That's not translation, and I don't think readers would get the same book.

Let me end with something hopeful. The number of translated novels published in English has risen steadily over the last decade, and they sell better than many people predicted. Readers, it seems, are curious about the world. And as long as they are, there'll be a need for people who care deeply about carrying a book across from one language to another.
Thank you. I think we've got time for a few questions.

title: Too Many Visitors?

lines.text: Right, Leo, we need to get these recommendations to the council by Friday, and I don't think we've agreed on a single thing yet.
That's slightly unfair. We agreed the coffee in this building is terrible.
True. Okay, let's go through the options. The tourist tax first. I'm inclined to support it: a small nightly charge, say two or three euros, ring-fenced for cleaning and maintaining the old town.

I was in favour too, initially. But I've been looking at the figures, and the problem is that a large proportion of our visitors don't stay overnight. Day-trippers, coach tours, cruise passengers: they make up roughly sixty per cent of visitors, and a hotel tax wouldn't touch them.
Hmm, that's a fair point. So it would penalise the very people who actually spend money here.
Exactly. Overnight guests eat in restaurants and visit museums. Day-trippers tend to walk round the cathedral, buy an ice cream and leave.
What about an entry fee for the old town, then, like some places have tried?

I'm not opposed in principle, but I'd want to see evidence that it actually reduces numbers rather than just raising money. From what I've read, the results elsewhere are mixed at best. And there's something uncomfortable about charging people to walk into what is, after all, a place where people live.

I'm less bothered by that than you are, I think. Residents would be exempt, obviously. But I take the point about evidence. Maybe we recommend a pilot, summer weekends only, and measure the effect properly.
I could live with a pilot. Now, cruise ships. That's where I feel more strongly.
Go on.
On days when two or three ships arrive, you get several thousand people arriving in the old town within the same hour. The streets simply can't cope. I'd cap it at one large ship per day.
I agree with the principle, but the port authority will fight that very hard, and they're not under the council's control. We might get further by negotiating staggered arrival times.
Which would help with the crowding, though not with the overall numbers. Still, it's realistic. Okay, staggered arrivals, with a cap as a longer-term goal.

Good. And then there's housing. Honestly, for residents, I think this is the real issue. The number of flats in the old town rented out to tourists has nearly tripled in eight years, and young families can't afford to live there anymore.
I completely agree, and it's the one I'd put first. A town where nobody actually lives becomes a kind of theme park. I'd suggest a freeze on new licences for holiday rentals in the historic centre.
A freeze rather than a ban?
Banning them outright would end up in court for years. A freeze is legally much safer, and it stops the problem growing while we work out a longer-term plan.
Agreed. So, in order of priority: housing first, then cruise arrivals, then the entry-fee pilot. And we drop the hotel tax?
Not drop it. Park it. It might make sense as part of a broader package later.
Fine, we'll park it. I'll draft the summary tonight and send it over.
